scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Batusi emerged in 1960s American television culture as a playful variation of the Watusi, a hugely popular dance craze of the era.
It made its screen debut on January 12, 1966, during 'Hi Diddle Riddle', the premiere episode of the Batman television series.
It appeared again three months later in the episode 'The Pharaoh's in a Rut', broadcast on April 14, 1966.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally staged for comic effect within a television narrative, the Batusi quickly exploded into a national dance craze across 1960s dance halls.

Over subsequent decades, it transitioned from a fad into a widely recognized pop-culture trope, referenced and parodied in animated series such as The Simpsons, Pinky and the Brain, and The Lego Batman Movie, as well as live-action shows like Xena: Warrior Princess and Titans.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The defining upper-body mechanic of the Batusi is performed by forming a horizontal V-sign using the index and middle fingers of both hands.
The dancer holds the palms toward the face and draws the fingers horizontally past the eyes, moving away from the center of the face simultaneously so that the eyes pass roughly between the fingers.
This motion is repeated in time with the music.
Watch for Eye Swipe V-Sign.

Formation: Solo informal floor space.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: As a novelty go-go style, the Batusi is danced to 1960s rock and roll, surf guitar, pop, or go-go discothèque music.

Its namesake roots tie directly to early-1960s hit singles, notably 'The Wah-Watusi' recorded by The Orlons in 1962 (and later covered by Chubby Checker), as well as Ray Barretto's 1963 Latin jazz hit 'El Watusi'.
Listen for the Electric guitar, Bass guitar, Drums, Brass section.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 120 beats a minute.
Mid-tempo 1960s pop and go-go music characterized by electric surf guitar, steady drum kits, and lively brass accents.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The Batusi requires no specific traditional attire, though its iconic origins place it within the context of 1960s discothèques and television studios, originally performed by Adam West in full Batman costume.
In casual social settings, it is performed as an informal solo or party go-go dance.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Adam West played a central role in popularizing the Batusi on television and claimed credit in 2005 for creating its distinct gestures.
Dance instructor Arthur Murray is also cited in historical accounts as the potential choreographer behind the routine.
While the core gesture remains identical, variants exist primarily in pop-culture adaptations.
The Batusi is a direct derivative subclass of 1960s go-go dancing inspired by the Watusi dance craze of the early 1960s.

narration: Before we go, one step. Form a horizontal V-sign with the index and middle fingers of both hands, palms facing toward your face.
Position your fingers in front of your eyes so your eyes look between the V-shape.
Count it: 1-2-3-4 then 5-6-7-8 (eight counts, two bars).

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Form a horizontal V-sign with the index and middle fingers of both hands, palms facing toward your face.
Step 2: Position your fingers in front of your eyes so your eyes look between the V-shape.
Footwork from the sources: Simple rhythmic weight shifts, 1960s go-go stepping or foot tapping on the beat.
Drill: Practice forming the horizontal V-sign with palms facing inward.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Draw both hands outward away from the center of the face horizontally in time with the music beat.
Step 4: Maintain a continuous rhythmic go-go step or torso twist with the lower body.
Drill: Draw fingers slowly across the eyes on beat counts 1-2 and 3-4.
